Objectives

After completing this course students will be able to: 

  • describe relevant theories and concepts in epistemology and philosophy of science. (Knowledge)
  • explain theories about the nature and cultural authority of science (Understanding)   
  • construct and to assess a philosophical argument relating to thinking about science. (Application)    
  • examine the distinction between science and pseudo-science. (Analysis)   
  • appraise philosophical claims about science. (Evaluation)    
  • develop an informed and nuanced view on science. (Synthesis)

In this course students will learn to think critically about what science is based on theories and concepts of philosophy of science, to understand what makes cultural studies scientific, to reflect upon philosophical and scientific theories and concepts, and to assess the role of science in society and (digital) culture. Students will thereby not only improve their understanding of the nature of science and of their own discipline as a scientific study. They will also learn to take a critical stance and develop the intellectual skills necessary for adequately dealing with the mass of information that we are flooded with these days.

The course consists of four sections. The first three sections form an introduction to the main concepts and theories in philosophy of science. The first section covers the debates concerning the sources of knowledge in antiquity and modernity, the scientific revolution, Hume’s challenge to scientific knowledge, and Kant’s solution to the rationalism-empiricism debate. The second section provides an overview of the most important debates in philosophy of science concerning the nature and the explanatory power of science. The third section presents new and powerful perspectives on the nature and value of scientific knowledge, like pragmatism and naturalism. In the final section of the course, we will apply what we learned about science to think critically about science as a culture and its implications, the relation between the humanities, the social sciences, and the natural sciences, and the cultural authority of science. Note: these are not the topics per lecture, but rather the topics that will be discussed in the course.

Program
PART I Basic Introduction to Philosophy of Knowledge

  1. Rationalism and Empiricism in Antiquity
  2. The Scientific Revolution
  3. Modern Rationalism and Empiricism
  4. The Limits of Science: Hume and Kant

PART II Introduction to Contemporary Philosophy of Science

  1. Logical Positivism and Falsificationism
  2. Language Games and Paradigms
  3. Research Programmes and Methodological Anarchism
  4. Realism and Belief in Science

PART III New Perspectives on Thinking about Science and Man          

  1. Pragmatism
  2. Naturalism

Part IV Thinking critically about science

  1. Science as a culture
  2. The humanities, the social sciences, and the natural sciences
  3. The cultural authority of science

Extra reading material will be announced and made available in due course.


Seminars

During the seminars we will recapitulate, think about and discuss the material that we covered during the lectures in an interactive way.  The seminars also provide the ideal opportunity for students to pose any further questions they have about the content of the course. Attendance is not compulsory but highly recommended.


Exams

There will be a mid-term and an end-term, both for 50% of your grade. The mid-term will cover the material discussed before then, the end-term is about the material covered since the midterm. There will be a separate resit for the mid-term and the end-term. Example questions and answers will be made available on Canvas and discussed in the seminars.


Final score

You do not have to pass each component, they can balance out one another. The final grades will be rounded as follows:


<.25 then rounded down to 0 (e.g. 8.24 -> 8.0)

.25 - .74 then rounded to 0.5 (e.g. 6.66 -> 6.5)

≥.75 then rounded up (e.g. 7.76 -> 8)


Except when you score between 5 and 6. A student cannot receive a 5.5 as a final grade, so rounding will be as follows:


<5.5 then 5

≥5.5 then 6


InfoSkills Tutorial & Test

As part of this course, you are required to complete the online library InfoSkills for Humanities and Digital Sciences.


The InfoSkills tutorial consists of five modules in which you will learn:

  1. how to recognize academic information; 
  2. where to find academic information;
  3. how to conduct effective searches; 
  4. how to use the library catalog;
  5. how to search library databases relevant to your program.

The tutorial ends with a 25-question test. Completing the tutorial will take you approximately 3 hours.
